caption: 2025 was a year of growth and healing and finding my footing again, with plenty of side quests along the way. I’ve been pretty quiet on here for most of it, but I’m still around, still digging, still collecting tees from bands most people have never heard of. If time allows before the year’s up, I’ll share some of my favorite finds. Starting with this unreal long sleeve from one of Raleigh’s finest exports, The Veldt.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '12 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: Continuing with some of my favorite finds from the year, here’s a late 80s Mission of Burma tee. It was released after the band had already broken up, during the period when Taang! Records held the rights to their catalog. The shirt was sold in limited quantities through Taang mail order, making it one of the oldest and rarest Burma tees out there.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '12 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: Next up from my top finds of 2025, the elusive Fun & Games basketball tee from Raleigh legends The Connells. Printed in a small run of about 50 in 1989 and sold at just a handful of shows, it reflects a time when college rock and college basketball shaped the culture across North Carolina, often intersecting.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '12 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: As it turns out, my top finds of 2025 include a few GBV tees, and this one stands out. It’s a one-time gig tee from the band’s 2002 show at the Dublin Pub in Dayton. The front graphic, which also served as the show poster, borrows the iconic Keith Richards “Drug Free America” photo. After this show, Bob was nearly arrested and GBV was banned from ever entering the Dublin Pub again.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '11 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: One of my favorite finds from 2025 came together in a pretty unexpected way. I typically do my sourcing in person — partly by choice, partly because I already spend enough time online — but every so often I’ll scroll the usual reselling apps. One night, I decided to open the particularly awful Goodwill app and search “band”. Imagine my surprise when this Band of Susans “The World and the Flesh” tee (an actual grail of mine) popped up with less than an hour left in the auction. Sometimes it really is just timing and luck.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '11 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: I’ve decided to keep sharing my favorite finds of 2025 until I get bored. After that, who knows. Maybe I’ll go silent for another year. Anyway, I’d been hunting for an Erectus Monotone tee for years, and 2025 finally delivered. Designed and printed by Tannis Root in the early 90s, it captures a specific moment in time from band whose potential outpaced their window.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '11 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: This one isn’t for everyone, and that’s kind of the point. The Pooh Sticks were deliberately opaque, built around anonymity and fictional personas as an artistic choice rather than a marketing move. There’s no real evidence that Gorillaz took direct inspiration from them, since both owe more to The Archies and earlier fictional acts than to each other, but they were operating on adjacent DNA. I’ve always thought the best power pop comes with a sense of irony, made by artists who don’t take themselves too seriously, and no one embodied that better than the Pooh Sticks. This rare tee features Paul (yes, just Paul), wearing his MC5 shirt, pulled from The Great White Wonder artwork by Alan Forbes during his Hanna-Barbera years.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '11 weeks ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption: further were one of those bands that thrived in the messy middle of the early 90s indie scene, with a lo-fi sound that was loose, noisy, and surprisingly melodic underneath it all. They couldn’t quite avoid the Dinosaur Jr. comparison, which wasn’t totally wrong, but it undersold how ragged and distinctive they really were. This is the only further tee I’ve ever seen and it just feels right: simple, a little odd, and not trying too hard.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '1 week ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption:
A great EP feels like a time capsule, catching a band at exactly the right moment, before anything gets smoothed out or lost along the way. Rougher, weirder, hungrier, more locked in. Pure essence. That’s what Archers of Loaf’s ...vs the Greatest of All Time has always felt like to me. It still has the energy of early Archers, but you can hear them stretching a little too, already reaching past the first record without letting go of that sound. It sits in that sweet spot between Icky Mettle and Vee Vee, where both impulses are still colliding.

And since nobody asked, my top 5 EPs from the 90s (in no particular order):

Archers of Loaf - ...vs the Greatest of All Time
Pavement - Watery, Domestic
Guided by Voices - Fast Japanese Spin Cycle
Sugar - Beaster
Modest Mouse - Interstate 8

Oh yeah, the t-shirt. Maybe the greatest Archers of Loaf tee ever made, for maybe the greatest EP ever made, featuring some hockey player named King Clancy.
notes: Approximate date inferred from '4 days ago' relative to March 23, 2026.

caption:
Some bands appreciate in ways you don’t quite see coming. This is my second time owning this Polvo tee, and the first time around, mid-pandemic, nobody seemed to care too much about Polvo shirts. A lot has changed since then, and it feels like more people keep finding their way to Polvo.

If you’re into 90s indie rock, the Chapel Hill scene, math rock, or just noisy guitars in general, Polvo are hard to miss. They’ve always been huge in that world, but they still never felt to me like the most obvious candidates for an afterlife thirty years later. Then again, we’re living in a moment where the Mountain Goats can soundtrack a TikTok dance, a Pavement B-side can become a generational hit, and Duster can take on a whole new life. The old boundaries of who gets remembered just don’t hold the way they used to.

A lot of bands get called lo-fi, but the Grifters always felt a little more warped than that. Darker too. They didn’t just bury melody under static, they messed with it and bent it into stranger shapes. Even at the messy breaking point, there was still something catchy underneath it all, the torn up and bruised remains of pop sensibility.

That’s what I’ve always liked about them. Lo-fi never felt like just a production choice for the Grifters. It felt built into the songs themselves. They sounded like a band that loved pop too much to leave it alone, and knew exactly how much damage a song could take and still survive.

#thegrifters

The story of Propeller is easy to romanticize, but the truth is already good enough. It’s one of the great love stories in rock and roll. A final record from a band with day jobs, no money, and just enough belief in themselves to give it one more shot when common sense probably said otherwise.

Even the fake GBV chant at the start feels important now. It sounds like a band trying to imagine its own future before anyone else could see it. But belief and reality don’t always line up, and the record didn’t land the way they hoped. Of the initial 500 pressings, a lot of copies sat unsold for a long time, unheard in Bob’s basement. The band broke up.

That could have been the end of the story. But it wasn’t. Instead, it became the start of a new one. Eventually copies of Propeller made their way to the right people, and things took off. What was meant to be the final statement somehow ended up being the opening line. It’s hard not to be romantic about the story of Propeller.

#guidedbyvoices
